docs.title: 🚀 Welcome to Nestify Documentation
docs.text:
Nestify is a fast, lightweight, cross-platform CLI written in Go. It helps you scan, analyze, contextualize for AI, scaffold, and clean-copy project structures — entirely offline, as a single native binary.

No Node.js. No Python runtime. No telemetry. Your code stays on your machine.

docs.title: ✨ What you can do
docs.text: Goal Command Start here Install the tool go install … Installation First useful results in minutes ignore-use → scan → context Quick Start Explore all CLI commands nestify --help Commands Overview AI-ready Markdown reports nestify context -p … AI Context Ignore & project templates ignore-use / init Templates How the code is organized — Architecture

docs.title: ⚡ 30-second path
docs.text:
# Install (once)
go install github.com/badboy1981/Nestify/cmd/nestify@latest

# Inside any project
nestify ignore-use go
nestify scan --tree -d 2
nestify context -p architecture -d 2

Reports are written under Nestify-Report/ in the current directory.

docs.title: 🧭 Documentation map
docs.text:
• Getting Started — install and quick start
  • CLI Commands — scan, ignore, analyze, context, prompt, init, copy
  • AI & Prompt Engineering — context reports and embedded prompts
  • Template & Ignore — ignore presets, scaffolding JSON, custom templates
  • Architecture — internal packages and request flow

docs.title: 🔒 Design principles
docs.text:
• Offline-first — scanning and report generation never call the network
  • Single binary — templates embedded with Go embed
  • Noise-aware — .nestifyignore keeps metrics and AI context token-efficient
  • Global CLI — run from any project folder after install

docs.title: Contributing to Nestify
docs.text:
Thanks for helping make Nestify better.

You can open an issue, suggest an idea, or implement a feature yourself. Either way: be respectful, keep changes focused, and tell us what cool capability you added so others can find and use it.

docs.title: Ways to contribute
docs.text:
Path When to use it Issue / feature request You have an idea or found a bug but cannot code it right now Pull request You implement the change in this repository Docs only Fix typos, clarify guides under docs/

If you open a PR, a short description of why the feature exists is more useful than a wall of implementation detail.

docs.title: Project shape (quick map)
docs.text:
cmd/nestify/main.go     → entrypoint, wires embedded templates into cli
internal/cli/           → subcommands, flags, user-facing messages
internal/<feature>/     → domain logic for that feature
templates-*/            → embedded ignore / project / prompt assets
docs/                   → MkDocs site

New capabilities almost always follow the same pattern already used by scan, copy, init, and the others.

docs.title: Adding a new command (standard path)
docs.text:
Yes — the usual approach is:

  1. Logic package under internal/ (e.g. internal/myfeature/)
  2. Handler under internal/cli/ (e.g. myfeature.go with runMyFeatureCmd)
  3. Register the subcommand in internal/cli/cli.go
  4. Update internal/cli/help.go (and docs when the feature is user-visible)
flowchart LR
    A[Idea / Issue] --> B[internal/feature package]
    B --> C[cli handler]
    C --> D[Register in cli.go]
    D --> E[Update help.go]
    E --> F[Optional: docs + README]
    F --> G[Open PR]

docs.title: Step-by-step
docs.text:
1. Implement the behavior in a dedicated package when the logic is non-trivial. Reuse existing pieces when they fit:

  • Path handling → internal/pathutil
  • Ignore rules → internal/ignore
  • Tree models → internal/types / internal/scanner

2. Add a CLI handler in internal/cli/, similar to scan.go or copy.go:

  • flag.NewFlagSet("mycommand", …)
  • Parse flags after os.Args[2:]
  • Call your package and print clear English status / error messages

3. Register in RunCli (internal/cli/cli.go):

case "mycommand":
    runMyFeatureCmd()

4. Document in --help (internal/cli/help.go) so nestify --help stays accurate.

5. (Recommended) Add a page under docs/commands/ and a line in mkdocs.yml / docs/commands/overview.md if users need more than a help line.

6. Build and try it locally:

go build -o nestify ./cmd/nestify
./nestify mycommand --help

docs.title: Templates without code changes
docs.text:
Ignore and prompt presets are loaded from the embedded filesystem by filename:

Folder Used by templates-ignore/*.txt ignore-list / ignore-use templates-prompts/*.txt prompt-list / prompt / context -p templates-projects/*.json init --template (and local paths)

Add a file, reinstall (go install ./cmd/nestify), and the new name appears — no switch statement required for listing.

docs.title: Style expectations
docs.text:
• User-facing messages and code comments in English (keeps the upstream codebase consistent)
  • Prefer small, focused PRs over giant refactors mixed with features
  • Match existing patterns (flag sets, emoji status lines, Nestify-Report/ for reports) unless you have a strong reason not to
  • Do not add network calls or telemetry to core paths; Nestify is offline-first by design

docs.title: Pull request checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Builds with go build ./cmd/nestify
  • [ ] New subcommand registered in cli.go and listed in help.go (if applicable)
  • [ ] Behavior respects .nestifyignore when the feature walks the tree (if applicable)
  • [ ] Docs updated when the change is user-visible
  • [ ] PR description states what you added and why it is useful

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
• Be kind in issues and reviews. Disagreement is fine; contempt is not.
  • Say clearly what you built or need — maintainers should not have to reverse-engineer your intent.
  • If something is experimental, label it that way.

Don't be an asshole. Ship useful work, explain it briefly, and leave the project easier to understand than you found it.

docs.text: By contributing, you agree that your contributions are licensed under the same terms as the project (see LICENSE in the repository root).

docs.title: 🏛️ Codebase Architecture & Internal Design
docs.text: Nestify is a small Go module (github.com/badboy1981/Nestify) compiled to one executable. Commands are dispatched from a thin CLI layer into focused internal packages.

docs.title: 📁 Repository layout
docs.text:
Nestify/
├── cmd/nestify/main.go          # Process entrypoint
├── embed.go                     # RootTemplatesFS (ignore / projects / prompts)
├── go.mod
├── internal/
│   ├── cli/                     # Flag parsing, user messages, command handlers
│   ├── scanner/                 # Directory walk → types.Node tree
│   ├── ignore/                  # IgnoreMatcher + template listing from embed.FS
│   ├── analyzer/                # Metrics & language breakdown
│   ├── treeprinter/             # ASCII tree strings
│   ├── generator/               # init: create folders/files from Node tree
│   ├── copier/                  # copy: stream files respecting ignore rules
│   ├── pathutil/                # OS path normalize + slash helpers
│   └── types/                   # Node, Template structs
├── templates-ignore/            # Embedded *.txt presets
├── templates-projects/          # Embedded *.json scaffolds
└── templates-prompts/           # Embedded prompt *.txt files

docs.title: 🚀 Startup flow
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[cmd/nestify/main.go] --> B[cli.SetTemplatesFS RootTemplatesFS]
    B --> C[cli.RunCli]
    C --> D{subcommand}
    D -->|scan| E[scanner + ignore]
    D -->|analyze / context| F[scanner + analyzer + treeprinter]
    D -->|ignore-list / ignore-use / prompt*| G[ignore + embed.FS]
    D -->|init| H[generator]
    D -->|copy| I[copier + ignore]
  1. main injects the embedded template filesystem into cli.
  2. RunCli switches on os.Args[1] (scan, context, copy, …).
  3. Each handler normalizes paths with pathutil, then calls the matching internal package.

docs.title: 📦 Package responsibilities
docs.text: Package Role cli Subcommands, flags, help/version, report file paths under Nestify-Report/ scanner Recursive walk with optional --depth and --folders-only; builds []types.Node ignore Loads .nestifyignore (+ built-in defaults); ShouldIgnore; lists templates from embed.FS analyzer File/folder counts, size, language stats → Markdown report body treeprinter Renders a Node as an ASCII tree string generator init: materializes folders/files (optional Content) from JSON nodes copier copy: walk source (cwd), stream file bytes to --path, same ignore rules pathutil NormalizeForOS, ToStandardPath for cross-platform paths types Shared Node and Template models

docs.title: 🧱 Core data model
docs.text:
// internal/types — simplified
type Node struct {
    Name     string
    Type     string // "folder" | "file"
    Content  string // used by init when present
    Size     int64
    Children []Node
}

type Template struct {
    ProjectType string
    Language    string
    Tags        []string
    Root        []Node
}
  • scan produces node trees (structure + sizes, not full file text).
  • init consumes JSON → generator.CreateStructure.
  • copy does not go through Node content; it streams real files via io.Copy.

docs.title: 🚫 Ignore pipeline
docs.text:
Shared by scan, analyze, context, and copy:

  1. ignore.NewIgnoreMatcher(target)
  2. Patterns from cwd .nestifyignore (and target’s file if different)
  3. Built-in defaults (e.g. .git, node_modules)
  4. ShouldIgnore(name) / ShouldIgnore(relativePath) during walk

ignore-use only writes a preset from templates-ignore/ onto disk as .nestifyignore.

docs.title: 📋 Command → code map
docs.text: Command Primary handlers / packages scan cli/scan.go → scanner → optional treeprinter analyze cli/analyze_handler.go → scanner + analyzer context cli/context_handler.go → scanner + analyzer + treeprinter + prompt helper ignore-list / ignore-use cli/ignore_handler.go → ignore + templatesFS prompt-list / prompt cli/prompt_handler.go → templatesFS init cli/init.go → generator copy cli/copy.go → copier → ignore --version cli/version.go

docs.title: 📦 Embedded templates
docs.text:
// embed.go
//go:embed templates-ignore templates-projects templates-prompts
var RootTemplatesFS embed.FS
  • Discovered by filename at runtime (no hard-coded name lists for ignore/prompt).
  • Adding a new .txt / keeping JSON under those folders + go install embeds them into the next binary.

docs.title: 🔐 Design constraints
docs.text:
• No network in core command paths
  • Single static-friendly binary (typical CGO_ENABLED=0 style Go CLI)
  • Cross-platform paths centralized in pathutil
  • CLI messages and comments in English for a consistent upstream codebase

docs.title: 💬 AI Context & Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
Nestify is built for local, offline-first AI workflows. It never sends your codebase to the cloud. Instead, it prepares a clean, token-efficient Markdown report that you can paste into any LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others).

The core idea is simple:

  1. Filter noise with .nestifyignore
  2. Generate a unified context report
  3. Optionally inject a focused prompt template
  4. Copy the report into your AI tool of choice

docs.title: 🧠 What the AI Context Report Contains
docs.text:
Running nestify context produces Nestify-Report/ai_context_report.md with:

Section Description AI Task & Instructions Optional header from -p (embedded template or custom text) Project Metrics Total size, file count, folder count Languages Breakdown Extension-based language distribution (GitHub-style bars) Project Directory Tree ASCII tree of the scanned structure

Because build artifacts and dependency folders are filtered out first, the report stays small and useful for LLM token limits.

docs.title: ⚡ Recommended AI Workflow
docs.text:
# 1. Reduce noise
nestify ignore-use go

# 2. Generate context with an architecture-focused prompt
nestify context -p architecture -d 2

# 3. Open the report and paste it into your LLM
#    Nestify-Report/ai_context_report.md

Run from anywhere

Open a terminal inside the project you want to analyze. Nestify works globally from any directory.

docs.title: 🛠️ Related Commands
docs.text: Command Role nestify context Build the unified AI-ready report nestify prompt-list List embedded prompt templates nestify prompt Print the full text of a template nestify ignore-use Apply tech-stack ignore rules before context

docs.title: 📋 Prompt Templates at a Glance
docs.text:
Nestify ships with embedded prompts under templates-prompts/:

  • default — general architecture review
  • architecture — Clean / Onion / Event-Driven checks
  • refactor — modular layout and coupling issues
  • security — structural AppSec risks
  • desktop — desktop app organization patterns

Full descriptions and usage are in Embedded Prompt Templates.

docs.title: ✏️ Custom Instructions
docs.text:
You are not limited to built-in templates. Pass any text to -p:

nestify context -p "Review this Go project for hexagonal architecture violations" -d 3

If the value matches a template name, that template is injected. Otherwise the string is used as a custom instruction block at the top of the report.

docs.title: 🔒 Privacy
docs.text:
• All scanning and report generation run locally
  • No telemetry
  • No network calls from Nestify itself
  • You decide what leaves your machine when you paste the report into an LLM

docs.title: ➡️ Next Steps
docs.text:
• Browse the prompt template catalog
  • Read the full context command reference
  • Start from the Quick Start if you have not run Nestify yet

docs.title: 📋 Embedded Prompt Templates
docs.text:
Nestify includes a set of prompt engineering templates embedded in the binary via Go’s embed package (templates-prompts/). They are injected into the top of ai_context_report.md when you use nestify context -p <name>.

You can also inspect any template in the terminal without generating a full report.

docs.title: 🧭 Discover & Inspect
docs.text:
# List all embedded prompt templates
nestify prompt-list

# Print the full instruction text of one template
nestify prompt architecture

docs.title: 📚 Template Catalog
docs.text: Content below matches the embedded files in templates-prompts/.

docs.title: default
docs.text:
Use when: you want a general architectural review.

You are an expert software architect and senior code reviewer.
Analyze the provided project directory structure and metrics report.
Provide a high-level architectural evaluation, highlight potential structural smells or organizational issues, and offer practical suggestions for improvement.

nestify context -p default

docs.title: architecture
docs.text:
Use when: checking Clean Architecture, Onion Architecture, or Event-Driven layering.

You are an enterprise software architect experienced in Clean Architecture, Onion Architecture, and Event-Driven systems.
Evaluate the directory and module structure of this project.
Verify layer separation (Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Presentation), check for dependency inversion violations, and suggest structural corrections to strictly maintain architectural boundaries.

nestify context -p architecture -d 2

docs.title: refactor
docs.text:
Use when: looking for coupling, misplaced modules, or a cleaner modular layout.

You are a senior software engineer specializing in code refactoring, clean code, and performance optimization.
Review the attached codebase tree and file distribution metrics.
Identify tightly coupled structures, misplaced modules, or overly complex directory layouts, and suggest a cleaner, refactored layout following modular design principles.

nestify context -p refactor

docs.title: security
docs.text:
Use when: reviewing structural exposure risks (configs, secrets layout, sensitive paths).

You are a cybersecurity expert and Application Security (AppSec) auditor.
Review the file structure and organizational components of this project.
Identify exposure risks (e.g., exposed configs, unhandled sensitive file extensions, or improper secrets segregation) and provide actionable security recommendations.

nestify context -p security -d 3

docs.title: desktop
docs.text:
Use when: reviewing desktop / cross-platform application organization.

You are a desktop application specialist (Windows / Linux / macOS cross-platform systems).
Analyze the project tree and code organization.
Check UI/Logic separation, multi-threading or async operational patterns, local resource/asset management, and platform-specific deployment readiness.

nestify context -p desktop

docs.title: ✏️ Custom Prompt Text
docs.text:
If -p does not match a template name, Nestify treats the value as custom instruction text:

nestify context -p "Focus on API boundaries and module ownership in this service" -d 2

If the value matches an embedded template name, that template is loaded. Otherwise the string is used as-is at the top of the report.

docs.title: 🔄 How Injection Works
docs.text:
1. You run nestify context -p <template-or-text>.
  2. Nestify resolves the prompt (embedded file or custom string).
  3. If a prompt is present, the report starts with:
# 💬 AI Task & Instructions

<prompt text here>

---
  1. Then metrics, language breakdown, and the directory tree follow.

Details of flags and output path: Context command.

docs.title: ➕ Adding Your Own Templates
docs.text:
Templates are loaded dynamically from templates-prompts/*.txt. No code change is required to register a new name.

  1. Add a file, for example templates-prompts/my-audit.txt, with the instruction text.
  2. Reinstall so the file is embedded into the binary:
go install ./cmd/nestify
  1. Confirm it appears:
nestify prompt-list
nestify prompt my-audit
nestify context -p my-audit

docs.title: 🧠 Analyze Command (nestify analyze)
docs.text:
The analyze command evaluates the overall structure of your project directory. It strips out build artifacts using .nestifyignore, calculates source-code language distribution based on real files, and aggregates directory metrics (file counts, folder counts, and total size).

It also outputs a compact, prompt-ready JSON summary intended for immediate copy-pasting into Large Language Model (LLM) workflows.

docs.title: 🛠️ Usage & Options
docs.text: nestify analyze [options]

docs.title: Flags & Options
docs.text:
Flag Short Description Default --path -p Target directory path to analyze. . (Current Directory) --depth -d Limits directory analysis depth (0 for unlimited). 0

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh). Learn more about Shell Agnostic Execution.

docs.title: 1. Analyze Current Working Directory
docs.text:
Evaluates the current project layout and saves the report to Nestify-Report/skeleton_report.md.

nestify analyze

docs.title: 2. Limit Traversal Depth
docs.text:
Restricts analysis and language breakdown to top-level project directories up to depth level 2.

nestify analyze -d 2

docs.title: 3. Analyze External Project Path
docs.text:
Targets any external repository path without navigating away from your working directory.

nestify analyze --path ./projects/MyDotNetApp -d 3

docs.title: 📄 Output Overview (skeleton_report.md)
docs.text: When nestify analyze finishes running, it creates a structured report inside the Nestify-Report/ folder containing project metrics, visual language progress bars, and a prompt-ready JSON summary.

docs.title: ⚙️ Language Breakdown Logic
docs.text: Nestify scans file extensions throughout your project while adhering strictly to .nestifyignore. By suppressing heavy third-party dependencies (node_modules/, vendor/, bin/, obj/), the language statistics accurately reflect your custom codebase composition rather than generated or external code.

docs.title: 💬 AI Context Generation (nestify context)
docs.text:
The context command is Nestify's primary tool for Prompt Engineering and LLM Contextualization. It merges project metrics, source code language breakdowns, and directory tree representations into a single, unified Markdown file (Nestify-Report/ai_context_report.md).

Additionally, it allows developers to inject pre-built or custom prompt instructions directly into the top of the report, making it instantly ready to send to LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini.

docs.title: 🛠️ Usage & Options
docs.text: nestify context [options]

docs.title: Flags & Options
docs.text:
Flag Short Description Default --prompt -p Injects an embedded prompt template (e.g. architecture, refactor, security) or raw instruction text into the report header. "" (None) --depth -d Limits directory tree traversal depth (0 for unlimited). 0 --path Target directory path to process. . (Current Directory)

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh). Learn more about Shell Agnostic Execution.

docs.title: 🔍 Discovering & Inspecting Prompt Templates
docs.text:
Before injecting a prompt template into nestify context, you can discover available presets or preview their exact text using the built-in prompt management tools:

  • List all embedded prompt templates: 

    nestify prompt-list

  • Inspect a specific prompt's instruction text: 

    nestify prompt architecture

For full details on using and customizing prompt instructions, check out the Prompt Management Guide.

docs.title: 1. Generate Standard AI Context (No Injected Prompt)
docs.text:
Scans the current project, analyzes language breakdown, builds the folder tree, and exports ai_context_report.md.

nestify context

docs.title: 2. Inject Built-in Prompt Template with Depth Restriction
docs.text:
Uses the embedded architecture prompt template and restricts tree depth to 3 levels deep.

nestify context -p architecture -d 3

(Available embedded prompts can be discovered using nestify prompt-list).

docs.title: 3. Inject Custom Prompt Text Directly
docs.text:
Passes a custom task instruction directly from your terminal CLI session:

nestify context -p "Review this codebase structure for Go clean architecture guidelines" -d 3

docs.title: 🤖 Prompt Processing Resolution Order
docs.text:
When you use the -p or --prompt flag, Nestify resolves the prompt input using the following logic:

  1. Embedded Template Match: It checks whether the string matches an embedded template file inside templates-prompts/ (e.g., refactor, security, architecture)[cite: 6]. If a match is found, the template's file content is injected[cite: 6].
  2. Raw Text Fallback: If no template name matches the provided argument, Nestify treats the input as raw custom prompt text and injects it as-is into the header[cite: 6].

docs.title: 📋 Clean Project Copy (nestify copy)
docs.text:
The copy command creates a clean physical copy of the current project into a new destination path. It walks the source directory, respects .nestifyignore rules, and streams every non-ignored file and folder to the target — including text and binary files.

Unlike init (which scaffolds an empty structure from JSON), copy transfers real file contents.

docs.title: 🛠️ Usage & Options
docs.text: nestify copy --path <destination>

docs.title: Flags & Options
docs.text:
Flag Short Description Default --path Destination directory for the clean copy. Required. —

Source is always the current directory

Nestify runs from the folder you are in. Open a terminal inside the project you want to clone, then point --path at the destination. There is no separate source flag.

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh).

docs.title: 💡 Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
1. Open a terminal inside the source project.
  2. Apply an ignore template (and customize .nestifyignore if needed):
nestify ignore-list
nestify ignore-use go
  1. Optionally inspect what will remain after filtering:
nestify scan --tree -d 2
  1. Copy the clean project to a new location:
nestify copy --path ../clean-project

docs.title: 1. Basic clean copy
docs.text:
# Inside the project you like
nestify ignore-use nodejs
nestify copy --path ../my-clean-app

docs.title: 2. After customizing ignore rules
docs.text:
nestify ignore-use go
# Edit .nestifyignore to add extra patterns if needed
nestify copy --path ./sandbox/clean-clone

docs.title: ⚙️ How Copy Works
docs.text:
1. Source = current working directory.
  2. Destination = value of --path (must not be empty or .).
  3. Filter = IgnoreMatcher loaded from .nestifyignore in the source (plus the same built-in defaults used by scan).
  4. Transfer = recursive walk; directories are created with MkdirAll, files are streamed with io.Copy (text and binary).
  5. Safety checks:
  6. Source and destination must not be the same path.
  7. Destination must not sit inside the source tree (avoids recursive copy).

docs.title: 📊 Output
docs.text:
On success the CLI prints a short summary:

📂 Source : /path/to/source
📂 Target : /path/to/destination
⏳ Copying (respecting .nestifyignore)...

✅ Clean project copied successfully!
   📁 Dirs  : 12
   📄 Files : 48
   📍 Path  : /path/to/destination

docs.title: 🔄 Difference from init
docs.text: nestify copy nestify init Input Live project on disk JSON blueprint Output Real files + folders (content included) Empty scaffold structure Filter .nestifyignore N/A (template defines structure) Typical use Clean clone of an existing repo Bootstrap from template / scan JSON

docs.title: ⚠️ Notes
docs.text:
• --path is required. Running nestify copy without it shows an error and a usage example.
  • Filtering decisions come only from .nestifyignore (and the matcher defaults already used elsewhere in Nestify). The command does not invent extra ignore rules.
  • Existing files in the destination may be overwritten when paths collide; choose an empty or new target folder when possible.

docs.title: 🚫 Ignore Management (ignore-list & ignore-use)
docs.text:
The Ignore System is the cornerstone of Nestify's noise-reduction engine. Before generating architecture reports or sending context to Large Language Models (LLMs), filtering out build artifacts, compiled binaries, dependency directories, and temporary OS files is critical to preserve token efficiency and report clarity.

Nestify provides embedded, zero-configuration ignore templates for 18+ major tech stacks.

docs.title: 🛠️ Commands Reference
docs.text: Nestify offers two primary commands to inspect and apply ignore templates:

docs.title: 1. List Available Templates (ignore-list)
docs.text:
Displays all tech-stack ignore templates built directly into the Nestify binary.

nestify ignore-list

docs.title: 2. Apply a Template (ignore-use)
docs.text:
Copies the specified embedded template into a local .nestifyignore file in your current working directory.

nestify ignore-use <template-name>

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh). Learn more about Shell Agnostic Execution.

docs.title: Step 1: Discover Embedded Tech Stacks
docs.text:
Run ignore-list to see available technology presets (e.g., go, dotnet, nodejs, python, flutter, unity, etc.):

nestify ignore-list

Output Preview:

Available embedded ignore templates:
  - angular
  - docker
  - dotnet
  - flutter
  - general
  - go
  - java
  - kotlin
  - nodejs
  - php-laravel
  - python
  - react
  - ruby
  - rust
  - swift
  - terraform
  - unity
  - vue

docs.title: Step 2: Apply Template to Current Project
docs.text:
Select your tech stack to generate a local .nestifyignore file:

nestify ignore-use go

(Replace go with dotnet, nodejs, python, flutter, or any supported template name).

docs.title: ⚙️ How .nestifyignore Works
docs.text: When any scanning command (scan, analyze, or context) is executed, Nestify looks for a .nestifyignore file in the project root. It parses gitignore-style glob patterns to exclude matching paths during directory traversal.

docs.title: Example .nestifyignore File Content (dotnet template):
docs.text:
# Build outputs
bin/
obj/
out/

# Dependencies & IDEs
.vs/
.vscode/
*.user
*.suo

# Test results
TestResults/

docs.title: 📝 Customizing Local Ignore Rules
docs.text:
The created .nestifyignore file is a plain text file. You can open it in any text editor and append project-specific custom rules:

# Append custom internal logs or data folders
/data/local_cache/
*.tmp_log
Default Scanning Behavior

If no .nestifyignore file is present in your target directory, Nestify performs a full, unfiltered traversal and includes all files and folders in the generated report. To ignore build artifacts or system clutter, ensure you generate a .nestifyignore file using nestify ignore-use <template>.

docs.title: 🏗️ Project Generation (nestify init)
docs.text:
The init command is Nestify's scaffolding engine. It reads a JSON layout blueprint and physically creates the entire directory and file hierarchy on your file system.

It can be used with embedded project presets or with JSON reports generated by nestify scan to instantly clone directory architectures.

docs.title: 🛠️ Usage & Options
docs.text: nestify init [options]

docs.title: Flags & Options
docs.text:
Flag Short Description Default --template -t Path to the JSON structure template or blueprint file. Required --path -p Target destination folder where the structure should be scaffolded. . (Current Directory)

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh). Learn more about Shell Agnostic Execution.

docs.title: 1. Bootstrap Project from Embedded/Local Template
docs.text:
Scaffolds a standard Go project structure into a target directory (./MyNewApp):

nestify init --template templates-projects/go_standard.json --path ./MyNewApp

docs.title: 2. Architectural Reverse-Engineering (Scaffold from Existing Scan)
docs.text:
Recreate an empty directory layout blueprint captured from a scanned GitHub repository or existing project:

# Step 1: Scan an existing project folder-only
nestify scan --path ./ExistingApp --folders-only

# Step 2: Use the generated JSON report to create a brand new empty clone
nestify init --template Nestify-Report/ExistingApp_20260805_010000.json --path ./NewCleanApp

docs.title: 📋 JSON Template Structure Format
docs.text: The init command parses JSON blueprints built as nested node trees. Each object specifies a name, a type ("folder" or "file"), and an optional list of children nodes.

docs.title: Example JSON Blueprint (go_basic.json):
docs.text:
[
  {
    "name": "cmd",
    "type": "folder",
    "children": [
      {
        "name": "app",
        "type": "folder",
        "children": [
          {
            "name": "main.go",
            "type": "file"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    "name": "internal",
    "type": "folder",
    "children": [
      {
        "name": "config",
        "type": "folder"
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    "name": "README.md",
    "type": "file"
  }
]

docs.title: ⚙️ How Generation Works
docs.text:
1. Path Normalization: Nestify automatically normalizes OS-specific path slashes (/ vs \) for seamless cross-platform execution.
  2. Recursive Directory Creation: It creates parent folders first before generating nested subdirectories or empty placeholder files.
  3. Safe Execution: Existing files are preserved unless overwritten, preventing accidental data loss during scaffolding.
Creating Custom Templates

You can create your own custom JSON blueprints manually or save nestify scan outputs to build a library of reusable organization templates.

docs.title: 🛠️ CLI Commands Overview
docs.text:
Nestify provides a suite of fast, token-efficient, and cross-platform command-line tools designed to streamline project structure scanning, codebase analysis, AI context generation, and project scaffolding.

All commands execute locally with zero network telemetry and share consistent syntax across Windows, macOS, and Linux.

docs.title: 🧭 Command Matrix at a Glance
docs.text: Command Primary Use Case Output Location Key Flags nestify scan Structural scanning to JSON node tree or Markdown tree. Nestify-Report/ --tree, -d, --folders-only nestify ignore-list Discover embedded tech-stack ignore presets. Terminal Output N/A nestify ignore-use Generate a local .nestifyignore file for noise reduction. .nestifyignore <template-name> nestify analyze Calculate language distribution percentages and project size metrics. skeleton_report.md -d, --path nestify context Generate a unified AI-ready Markdown context report with optional prompt injection. ai_context_report.md -p, -d, --path nestify prompt-list Discover built-in prompt engineering templates. Terminal Output <template-name> nestify init Scaffold empty physical directory/file structures from JSON blueprints. Target Path --template, --path nestify copy Copy current project to a new path with real file contents (respects .nestifyignore). Destination path --path

docs.title: ⚡ Recommended Workflow Sequence
docs.text:
To get the most out of Nestify, follow this standard execution order:

graph LR
    A[<b>1. Suppress Clutter</b><br/><code>nestify ignore-use <tech></code>] --> B{Choose Your Goal}

    B -->|AI Context & Prompts| C[<b>AI Analysis</b><br/><code>nestify context -p <prompt></code>]
    B -->|Directory Tree & JSON| D[<b>Visual Scan</b><br/><code>nestify scan --tree</code>]
    B -->|Language Breakdown| E[<b>Code Metrics</b><br/><code>nestify analyze</code>]
    B -->|Clean Clone| F[<b>Clean Copy</b><br/><code>nestify copy --path <dest></code>]

  1. Suppress Clutter First: Run nestify ignore-use <tech-stack> to filter out compiled binaries, dependencies, and temporary files (bin/, obj/, node_modules/).

  2. Contextualize for AI: Run nestify context -p <template> to generate a complete codebase context report merged with custom LLM task instructions.

  3. Inspect Architecture: Run nestify scan --tree -d 2 to review high-level directory organization without drowning in file details.

  4. Clean Clone (optional): Run nestify copy --path ../clean-project to copy the filtered project (real files + folders) to a new location.

docs.title: 🌐 Cross-Platform Parity
docs.text:
Nestify is compiled into a single native binary using Go. It requires no external runtime dependencies (Node.js, Python, or .NET).

Terminal & Shell Support

All syntax, flags, and outputs function identically across Windows (PowerShell, Command Prompt), macOS (Terminal, iTerm), and Linux (Bash, Zsh). File paths are automatically normalized across OS-specific separators (/ vs \).

docs.title: 💬 Prompt Management (prompt-list & prompt)
docs.text:
Nestify comes with a set of embedded, pre-built Prompt Templates designed for common LLM codebase analysis tasks (e.g., Clean Architecture checks, refactoring guides, security audits, and desktop app code reviews).

The prompt management commands allow you to discover available embedded prompts and inspect their exact text directly from your terminal.

docs.title: 1. List Available Prompts (prompt-list)
docs.text:
Displays all prompt templates built directly into the Nestify binary.

nestify prompt-list

docs.title: 2. View Prompt Content (prompt)
docs.text:
Prints the full instruction text of a specific embedded prompt template to the console.

nestify prompt <template-name>

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh). Learn more about Shell Agnostic Execution.

docs.title: Step 1: List Built-in Prompt Templates
docs.text:
Run prompt-list to view all available prompt presets:

nestify prompt-list

Output Preview:

Available embedded prompt templates:
  - architecture
  - default
  - desktop
  - refactor
  - security

docs.title: Step 2: Inspect a Template's Content
docs.text:
Before injecting a prompt template into nestify context, you can preview its exact wording:

nestify prompt architecture

Output Preview:

You are an enterprise software architect experienced in Clean Architecture, Onion Architecture, and Event-Driven systems.

Verify layer separation (Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Presentation), check for dependency inversion violations, and suggest structural corrections to strictly maintain architectural boundaries.

Once you know the name of your desired template, pass it to the context command using the -p flag:

nestify context -p architecture -d 2

docs.title: 🔍 Scan Command (nestify scan)
docs.text: The scan command is the core structural scanner of Nestify. It recursively traverses a project directory, applies .nestifyignore rules to strip out build clutter and binary artifacts, and generates structured outputs in both JSON and Markdown Tree formats.

docs.title: 🛠️ Usage & Options
docs.text: nestify scan [options]

docs.title: Flags & Options
docs.text:
Flag Short Description Default --path -p Target directory path to scan. . (Current Directory) --tree Generates a human-readable ASCII tree report (.md). false --folders-only Restricts traversal to directories, ignoring all files. false --depth -d Limits directory traversal depth (0 for unlimited). 0

Cross-Platform & Shell Agnostic

Nestify is compiled into a single native binary with zero external dependencies. All CLI commands run identically across Windows (PowerShell / CMD), macOS, and Linux (Bash / Zsh). Learn more about Shell Agnostic Execution.

docs.title: 1. Basic Directory Scan (JSON Output)
docs.text:
Scans the current working directory and saves a timestamped JSON node report inside (Nestify-Report/).

nestify scan

docs.title: 2. Generate a Visual Directory Tree
docs.text:
Produces both the default JSON report and a clean ASCII tree Markdown report (Nestify-Report/PROJECT_TIMESTAMP.md).

nestify scan --tree

docs.title: 3. High-Level Clean Architecture View
docs.text:
Excludes files from the scan to inspect only the folder hierarchy up to a depth level of 2.

nestify scan --folders-only -d 2

docs.title: 4. Scan a Specific External Path
docs.text:
Target any folder on your file system without leaving your current terminal working directory.

nestify scan --path ./projects/MyApi --tree -d 3

docs.title: 🔒 Ignore Logic Integration
docs.text:
The scan command automatically respects:

  1. Standard built-in default ignore patterns (.git/, .DS_Store, etc.).
  2. Project-level .nestifyignore files located in the target scanning directory.
Need to ignore language-specific build folders?

Run nestify ignore-use <tech-stack> before scanning to automatically suppress heavy folders like node_modules/, bin/, obj/, or vendor/.

docs.title: Binary install
docs.text:
Installation Guide Nestify can be installed either as a standalone pre-built binary or built directly from source using the Go toolchain. Select your preferred installation method below to view the detailed setup instructions.

=== "Pre-built Binary (binary.md)"# Pre-built Binary Installation

This guide walks you through downloading and configuring pre-compiled binaries for Nestify across supported operating systems.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before installing, ensure your system meets the minimum requirements:

  • Supported Operating Systems: Linux (amd64, arm64), macOS (Intel, Apple Silicon), Windows (x86_64)

  • Command Line Utilities: curl or wget for automated fetching, and tar or unzip for archive extraction

  • Permissions: Administrative or sudo access if installing into system-wide executable paths (such as /usr/local/bin)

docs.title: Automated Installation Script
docs.text:
The fastest method to install Nestify is using the automated installer script, which detects your OS and architecture automatically:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nestify/nestify/main/install.sh | bash

Customizing Destination Directory

By default, the automated installer targets /usr/local/bin. You can override the destination directory by supplying the BINDIR environment variable:

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nestify/nestify/main/install.sh | BINDIR=$HOME/.local/bin bash

docs.title: Manual Installation
docs.text:
If you prefer to download and verify binaries manually, follow these steps:

  1. Navigate to the official releases page and locate the latest release build.

  2. Download the package corresponding to your operating system and CPU architecture.

  3. Extract the archive contents:

docs.title: For Linux / macOS tarballs
docs.text: tar -xzf nestify_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz

docs.title: For Windows zip archives (PowerShell)
docs.text:
Expand-Archive -Path nestify_Windows_x86_64.zip -DestinationPath C:\nestify
  1. Move the executable to a directory listed in your system PATH:
sudo mv nestify /usr/local/bin/
  1. Verify the executable permissions and confirm successful installation:
nestify version

Checksum Verification

To ensure package integrity, compare the SHA-256 hash of your downloaded file against the published checksums.txt document:

    sha256sum --check checksums.txt 2>&1 | grep OK

docs.title: Permission Denied Errors
docs.text:
If executing nestify returns Permission denied (EACCES), grant execution rights explicitly:

chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nestify

docs.title: macOS Developer Verification Block
docs.text:
macOS Security may block unverified binaries with an "unidentified developer" prompt. You can strip the quarantine attribute using xattr:

xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /usr/local/bin/nestify

docs.title: Command Not Found
docs.text:
If running nestify results in command not found, verify that your destination folder exists within your shell's active $PATH:

echo $PATH

If necessary, append the installation directory to your profile file (~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc):

export PATH="$PATH:/usr/local/bin"

=== "Go / Source (go-install.md)"# Go / Source Installation

This document provides instructions for compiling and installing Nestify directly from source code using the Go toolchain.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure your local development setup satisfies the following dependencies: * Go Toolchain: Go 1.16 or higher installed (go version)

  • Git: Installed and available on your system path

  • Environment Configuration: Ensure $GOPATH/bin is exported in your environment PATH

Requirement Minimum Version Recommended Go Compiler 1.16.0 1.22+ Git 2.20.0 Latest Storage 50 MB 100 MB

Verifying Go Environment Variables

Confirm your GOPATH and GOBIN paths before running the module installation commands:

go env GOPATH GOBIN

docs.title: Installation via go install
docs.text:
To compile and install the executable directly into your $GOPATH/bin directory, run:

go install github.com/badboy1981/Nestify/cmd/nestify@latest

To install a specific tagged release version:

go install github.com/badboy1981/Nestify/cmd/nestify@v1.0.0

docs.title: Compiling from Source Repository
docs.text:
If you intend to modify the codebase or contribute to development, build the binary directly from the cloned repository:

  1. Clone the project repository:
git clone https://github.com/badboy1981/Nestify.git

cd Nestify
  1. Download and verify module dependencies:
go mod download

go mod verify
  1. Compile the binary using go install or go build:
go install ./cmd/nestify
  1. Verify the installed binary:
nestify --version

CGO Dependencies Notice

Nestify is designed to compile with CGO_ENABLED=0 by default to produce statically linked binaries. If cross-compiling or utilizing CGO features, ensure your local gcc or clang cross-compiler tools are properly configured.

docs.title: Binary Installed but Command Not Found
docs.text:
When go install succeeds but running nestify fails, your Go binary directory is not included in your active shell path. Add the GOBIN path to your shell configuration:

# For Zsh (~/.zshrc) or Bash (~/.bashrc)

export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

Reload the configuration in your active session:

source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Module Proxy and Download Errors
docs.text:
If network restrictions impede dependency retrieval during installation, set an explicit public Go proxy:

export GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct

go install github.com/badboy1981/Nestify/cmd/nestify@latest

docs.title: Clearing Build Caches
docs.text:
If you experience build irregularities or lingering artifact issues after upgrading Go versions, clear the build and module cache:

go clean -cache -modcache

docs.title: Nestify Go Installation Guide
docs.text: Comprehensive setup, dependency configuration, and deployment instructions for Nestify.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Nestify is built using Go (Golang) to leverage high-concurrency execution, cross-platform portability, and low resource overhead. This guide walks you through preparing your environment, installing the Go runtime, configuring system path variables, building Nestify from source or binary, and resolving common installation issues.

docs.text:
Ensure your host system meets or exceeds the minimum operating hardware and software requirements listed below before proceeding.

Component Minimum Requirement Recommended Specification Go Version Go 1.21.0 or higher Go 1.22.x or latest stable release Architecture amd64 (x86_64) or arm64 (Apple Silicon / AArch64) amd64 or arm64 Memory (RAM) 512 MB 2 GB+ Storage 250 MB free disk space 1 GB+ free disk space

docs.title: Step 1: Installing the Go Runtime Environment
docs.text: If Go is not already installed on your system, follow the platform-specific instructions below to install the official Go toolchain.

docs.title: macOS Installation
docs.text:
You can install Go on macOS using either Homebrew or the official installer package:

  • Option A: Using Homebrew (Recommended) Execute the following command in your terminal: brew install go
  • Option B: Official Installer Package Download the appropriate .pkg installer from the official Go download portal (go.dev) and run the setup wizard.

docs.title: Linux Installation
docs.text:
Download and extract the official Go binary tarball into system folders:

  • Download Archive: wget https://go.dev/dl/go1.22.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz
  • Extract Files: sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.22.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz
  • Configure User Path: Append export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin to your ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or profile configuration file.

docs.title: Windows Installation
docs.text:
• Download the MSI installer package (go1.22.x.windows-amd64.msi) from the official Go website.
  • Open the downloaded file and follow the GUI installation prompts.
  • The installer automatically registers Go binary paths into your system PATH environment variable.

docs.title: Step 2: Path Environment Variable Setup
docs.text: To enable global command execution for Go binaries installed via go install, append your local GOPATH binary folder to your system environment.

docs.title: Shell Path Configuration Matrix
docs.text:
| Shell / Operating System | Profile Configuration File | Command to Append | | Bash (Linux/macOS) | ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile | export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin | | Zsh (macOS/Linux) | ~/.zshrc | export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin | | PowerShell (Windows) | $PROFILE | $env:Path += ";$(go env GOPATH)\bin" |

Apply profile updates immediately by restarting your shell or running source ~/.zshrc (or source ~/.bashrc).

docs.title: Verifying Go Installation
docs.text:
To verify that Go is correctly installed and accessible in your command prompt, execute:

go versionExpected console output should resemble:

go version go1.22.5 darwin/arm64

docs.title: Step 3: Installing Nestify
docs.text: You can install Nestify using either the Go binary installer or by compiling directly from source code.

docs.title: Option A: Install via Go CLI (Recommended)
docs.text:
Run the command below to automatically download, compile, and place the executable into your GOPATH/bin directory:

go install github.com/nestify/nestify/cmd/nestify@latest

docs.title: Option B: Building from Source Repository
docs.text:
For development setups or customized compilation:

  • Clone the Repository: git clone https://github.com/nestify/nestify.git
  • Navigate to Project Root: cd nestify
  • Fetch Dependencies: go mod download
  • Compile Execution Binary: go build -o nestify ./cmd/nestify
  • Move Binary to Global Executable Path (Optional): sudo mv nestify /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: Step 4: Installation Verification
docs.text:
Confirm that Nestify is correctly installed and executable:

nestify --versionTo inspect supported command flags, configuration parameters, and subcommands, display the general help menu:

nestify --help

docs.title: Issue: "command not found: nestify"
docs.text:
• Cause: The binary output path $(go env GOPATH)/bin is missing from your system PATH environment variable.
  • Solution: Re-check Step 2 and ensure your shell profile exports $(go env GOPATH)/bin.

docs.title: Issue: Module Dependency / Checksum Mismatch
docs.text:
• Cause: Corrupted local Go module cache.
  • Solution: Clear the cache and re-download module dependencies: go clean -modcache go mod tidy

docs.title: Issue: Permission Denied During Installation
docs.text:
• Cause: Insufficient write permissions for standard system binary directories like /usr/local/bin.
  • Solution: Execute moving steps with sudo or modify target destination to user-owned binary paths such as ~/.local/bin or $(go env GOPATH)/bin.

docs.title: Documentation & Maintenance Contact
docs.text: For additional assistance, bug reports, or enterprise support regarding Nestify releases, contact Person or check repository maintenance updates from Date.

docs.title: ⚙️ Installation
docs.text:
Nestify is a fast, lightweight CLI tool compiled into a single native binary. It has zero external runtime dependencies — once installed, it runs completely offline. All ignore templates, project templates, and prompt templates are embedded directly into the binary via Go’s embed package.

You only need Go installed on your system (for the recommended method).

docs.title: 📋 Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Notes Go Required for Method 1. Project is built with Go 1.24 (compatible with Go 1.16+). Git Required only if you prefer to clone the repository. Supported platforms Windows, macOS, Linux (amd64 / arm64)

Zero External Runtimes

After installation Nestify is a standalone executable. No Node.js, Python, virtual environments, or extra daemons are needed.

docs.title: 🚀 Method 1 — Install with Go (Recommended)
docs.text: This is the most common and familiar way for developers who already have Go installed.

docs.title: Option A: One-line install (fastest)
docs.text: go install github.com/badboy1981/Nestify/cmd/nestify@latest

docs.title: Option B: Clone and install (useful for development)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/badboy1981/Nestify.git
cd Nestify
go install ./cmd/nestify

Both commands compile the binary (including all embedded templates) and place it in your Go binary directory ($(go env GOPATH)/bin).

docs.title: 📦 Method 2 — Pre-built Binary (GitHub Releases)
docs.text:
If you prefer not to use the Go toolchain, download a ready-made binary from the official releases page:

  1. Go to the Releases page.
  2. Download the archive that matches your operating system and architecture.
  3. Extract the archive.
  4. Move the nestify (or nestify.exe) executable to a directory that is already in your PATH (examples: /usr/local/bin, ~/.local/bin, or any custom folder you prefer).
  5. Make sure the file is executable (Linux / macOS):
chmod +x nestify

docs.title: ✅ Verify the Installation
docs.text:
Run the version command from any directory:

nestify --version

or

nestify version

Expected output:

Nestify v1.0.0
Build Date: 2025-12-31
Author: badboy1981
Repository: https://github.com/badboy1981/Nestify

A powerful project structure scanner, analyzer, and generator written in Go.
Use 'nestify --help' for usage information.

If you see this output, Nestify is ready to use.

docs.title: 🔧 Troubleshooting PATH Issues
docs.text: If the terminal says command not found or 'nestify' is not recognized, the directory containing the binary is missing from your PATH.

docs.title: Default Go binary locations
docs.text:
Operating System Default location Windows %USERPROFILE%\go\bin macOS / Linux $HOME/go/bin

You can always check the exact path with:

go env GOPATH

docs.title: Windows (PowerShell)
docs.text:
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", $env:Path + ";$env:USERPROFILE\go\bin", "User")

Restart the terminal after running the command.

docs.title: macOS / Linux (Zsh or Bash)
docs.text:
# For Zsh (default on modern macOS)
echo 'export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

# For Bash
echo 'export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

After updating the PATH, run nestify --version again to confirm.

docs.title: ➡️ Next Step
docs.text: Once Nestify is installed, continue to the Quick Start guide to run your first commands.

docs.title: ⚡ Quick Start
docs.text:
Nestify is installed and ready. Follow these short steps to get your first useful results in under two minutes.

Run from anywhere

Nestify works globally. Open a terminal inside any project folder and run the commands below. You can also target another path with --path ./some/folder.

docs.title: ✅ 1. Confirm the Installation
docs.text:
nestify --version

You should see the version information. You can also explore all available commands:

nestify --help

docs.title: 🧹 2. Remove Project Noise
docs.text:
Before scanning, apply an ignore template so build artifacts and dependency folders are filtered out.

nestify ignore-list

Then apply the template that matches your project:

nestify ignore-use go

Replace go with any other available template (nodejs, python, dotnet, flutter, …).

This creates a local .nestifyignore file in the current directory.

docs.title: 🌳 3. See the Folder Structure
docs.text:
Generate a clean, readable tree of your project:

nestify scan --tree -d 2

Useful scan parameters

  • --tree → produces a human-readable Markdown tree
  • -d 2 → limits scan depth to 2 levels
  • --folders-only → shows only folders (no files)

The report is saved inside the Nestify-Report/ folder.

docs.title: 🧠 4. Generate an AI-Ready Context Report
docs.text:
Create a unified Markdown report that combines metrics, language distribution, and the project tree — perfect for pasting into an LLM:

nestify context -p architecture -d 2
  • -p architecture injects the built-in architecture prompt template
  • You can also pass custom text: -p "Review this structure for clean architecture"

The output is saved as Nestify-Report/ai_context_report.md.

docs.title: 📊 5. Optional — Project Metrics
docs.text:
Get a quick overview of language distribution and project size:

nestify analyze

docs.title: 📁 Where Are the Reports?
docs.text:
All generated files are automatically placed in a Nestify-Report/ directory in your current working folder:

  • JSON structure reports
  • Markdown tree reports
  • ai_context_report.md
  • skeleton_report.md

docs.title: 🛠️ Custom Scaffolding & Project Templates
docs.text:
Project templates are JSON blueprints under templates-projects/. nestify init reads a blueprint and creates the physical folders and files on disk (including optional file content).

This is different from nestify copy, which clones a live project while respecting .nestifyignore.

docs.title: 🏗️ Built-in project templates
docs.text:
File Description go_basic.json Minimal Go layout (cmd/main.go, internal/) go_standard.json Standard-style Go layout (cmd, internal layers, pkg, configs, …) mkdocs_scaffold.json Documentation site skeleton for MkDocs-style docs/ trees

Paths are relative to the Nestify source tree when you clone the repo. After install, you can still point --template at any JSON file on disk (including scan exports under Nestify-Report/).

docs.title: 🛠️ Usage
docs.text:
nestify init --template <path-to-json> --path <destination>
Flag Description --template JSON blueprint path --path Where to create the structure (default .)

Example with an embedded-style path from a local clone:

nestify init --template templates-projects/go_standard.json --path ./MyNewApp

CLI reference: Init command.

docs.title: 📋 JSON shape
docs.text:
init unmarshals into the project Template type. The important field is root: a tree of nodes.

Each node:

Field Meaning name File or folder name type "folder" or "file" content Optional string written into files (empty → empty file) children Nested nodes (folders)

Example (simplified from go_basic.json):

{
  "name": "GoBasicProject",
  "root": [
    {
      "name": "cmd",
      "type": "folder",
      "children": [
        {
          "name": "main.go",
          "type": "file",
          "content": "package main\n\nimport \"fmt\"\n\nfunc main() {\n\tfmt.Println(\"Generated by Nestify!\")\n}"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "internal",
      "type": "folder"
    }
  ]
}

mkdocs_scaffold.json also sets projectType, language, and tags metadata fields.

docs.title: 🔄 Scaffold from a live project (structure only)
docs.text:
1. Scan folders only:
nestify scan --folders-only
  1. Use the generated JSON under Nestify-Report/ as --template:
nestify init --template Nestify-Report/YourProject_TIMESTAMP.json --path ./NewEmptyClone

This recreates structure (and empty files unless the JSON carries content). For a full clean copy with real file bytes, use nestify copy instead.

docs.title: ➕ Add your own project template
docs.text:
1. Author a JSON file following the node tree format above.
  2. Optionally place it in templates-projects/ inside a Nestify clone.
  3. Run init with --template pointing at that file.
  4. If you want it embedded for distribution, keep it under templates-projects/ and reinstall with go install ./cmd/nestify (same embed pattern as ignore/prompt templates).

docs.title: ⚖️ init vs copy
docs.text: init copy Input JSON blueprint Live directory (cwd) Output Scaffolded tree from template Real files streamed to --path Filter Defined by JSON .nestifyignore Best for New empty/skeleton projects Clean clone of an existing repo

docs.title: 🚫 Ignore Templates (.nestifyignore)
docs.text:
Ignore templates are plain-text rule lists embedded under templates-ignore/. nestify ignore-use <name> copies one of them to a local .nestifyignore in your current directory.

That file is then used by scan, analyze, context, and copy to skip build noise and dependency trees.

docs.title: 🛠️ Commands
docs.text:
# List every embedded ignore template
nestify ignore-list

# Apply a template (creates/overwrites ./.nestifyignore)
nestify ignore-use go

CLI details: Ignore Management.

docs.title: 📚 Available templates
docs.text:
Names match the embedded templates-ignore/*.txt files (without the extension):

Template Typical use general Generic OS / editor / VCS clutter go Go modules, binaries, coverage nodejs node_modules, npm/yarn caches python __pycache__, venv, dist dotnet bin/, obj/, Visual Studio java Maven/Gradle build outputs kotlin Kotlin / Android build noise react React / front-end build folders vue Vue CLI / Vite outputs angular Angular CLI caches and dist flutter Flutter / Dart build artifacts unity Unity Library, Temp, Builds rust target/ and Cargo artifacts ruby Bundler / Rails temp paths swift Xcode / SPM derived data php-laravel Laravel vendor and caches docker Docker-related local clutter terraform Terraform state and providers

Run nestify ignore-list on your installed binary for the authoritative list.

docs.title: ⚙️ How matching works
docs.text:
When a scan-style command runs, Nestify builds an IgnoreMatcher that:

  1. Reads .nestifyignore from the current working directory
  2. If --path points elsewhere, also reads that path’s .nestifyignore when present
  3. Adds built-in defaults already used by the matcher (including .git and node_modules)

Patterns are matched against base names and relative paths (similar to simple gitignore-style rules).

docs.title: 📝 Customize after apply
docs.text:
.nestifyignore is a normal text file. After ignore-use, edit it freely:

# Extra project-specific rules
/data/local_cache/
*.tmp_log
Nestify-Report/

Many templates already include commented optional blocks (for example Nestify self-ignore). Uncomment lines by removing the leading #.

docs.title: 🔄 Typical workflow
docs.text:
# Inside your project
nestify ignore-use nodejs
# Edit .nestifyignore if needed
nestify scan --tree -d 2
nestify context -p architecture -d 2
# Optional: clean physical copy
nestify copy --path ../clean-app

No ignore file

If there is no .nestifyignore, traversal is largely unfiltered (aside from matcher defaults). Always apply a template before serious AI context or copy work.

docs.title: ➕ Add a custom ignore template to the binary
docs.text:
1. Create templates-ignore/my-stack.txt with one pattern per line.
  2. Reinstall:
go install ./cmd/nestify
  1. Verify:
nestify ignore-list
nestify ignore-use my-stack

No Go code changes are required; templates are discovered dynamically from the embedded FS.
